mapping.note: failover-horizon two-mode automaton. Primary reading (A) = the IMPLEMENTATION text: a spot preemption makes the controller start the on-demand tail immediately and it latches there until the job finishes -> $139.20. Control reading (B) = the IDEA text ('tail scheduled as late as possible', no latch) -> $96.54 / -106.77, i.e. indistinguishable from the seed ($96.52 / -106.75). The 44% gap between the two readings is the single most expensive sentence in this task. cost_std 14.56 vs the seed's 40.92 is the fingerprint of the latch: the outcome no longer varies with trace quality.

mapping.note: conflict graph -> connected components -> per-component DAG longest path (op durations 1) -> NEH construction + iterated greedy with SA acceptance, d=max(2,n/5), 15 s wall-clock budget per workload. Per-workload split (234/51/69 vs the seed's 252/57/48): wins W1 and W2, loses W3. The proxy makespan is a MAX over components (unbounded parallel workers) while the ground truth get_opt_seq_cost is an additive lock-conflict simulation, so cross-component order is invisible to the optimiser. The wall-clock budget is what the solution prescribes, and it is the only source of run-to-run variation (the evaluator seeds the RNG with EVAL_SEED=2026). The reported makespan is the environment's ground-truth cost of the returned schedule, never the proxy value.

prefix-layout planner (modules 2/3/4): bounded-sample profiler with a character-length token proxy, greedy field order by score(f)=sum_G sum_v max(0,n(G,v)-1)*len(G,v) with live-group splitting (tau_min=8, G_max=512), remaining fields appended in original schema order, row order = prefix-trie DFS by (cnt_j desc, value_j asc). The whole gap is on PDMX (0.31972 vs the seed's 0.39680); the row order contributes nothing there (31.95 our rows / 31.97 full-row sort / 31.98 original rows) and a global greedy column order is worse still (29.47), so the loss is the solution's own last instruction: the fields after the k prefix fields keep their schema order, whereas the seed's GGR reorders every column at every recursion level. Runtime 10.4 s/dataset is 6.8x faster than the seed but the runtime term only pays 0.0067.

tree-column LP: candidate pool = direct multicast tree + a star through each relay region + two-hop relay variants with a fan-out partition + randomized greedy directed-Steiner trees (3-hop cap, perturbed costs), deduplicated by edge set; the LP keeps the cheapest tree and all partitions reuse it. The edge and per-VM capacity rows need bw(u,v), the per-VM caps and the deadline T, none of which the interface exposes, so every capacity row is slack and the LP degenerates to picking the cheapest column. -37.9% egress cost vs the seed (the seed pays for a shared edge once per destination). 2.1% more expensive than the paper-side solution, which solves the same 'one shared multicast tree' with an exact MILP over clustered, hop-limited edges instead of a candidate pool.

residency planner U_m=(Q_m + alpha*predicted_demand_m)*priority_m/(W_m + expected_KV_m) with a 5% staging buffer. Only W_m and req_rate are observable, so Q_m = predicted_demand_m = req_rate, priority_m = 1/slo, expected_KV_m = 0; 'cold models receive zero replicas' cannot be honoured because every model must be placed, and the activity split is taken from the solution's own queue-emptiness rule (req_rate > 0 for every shipped test case), so the planner degenerates to the spreading clause alone. Ablation: with the seed's ordering key (req_rate/slo) the same placement rule reproduces the seed bit-for-bit (21.891622105209393), and the 5% staging buffer is immaterial (19.7433 without it) - the entire gap is the extra division by W_m in the utility, which is the right key for 'what to keep resident' and the wrong key for min-max packing.
